chapter: Return to Atlanta and move north
title: Thrown off the whites-only train car
summary: Robey seats the boys in the white car, the conductor objects, and Robey gives up the tickets and buys a car.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: He bought a car. He was a funny man. He was a funny person too, you know. He liked Negroes, you see, and --

He was a fight promoter. He was about the popularist properest one in the South at the time, George Robey, because he had this heavyweight contender, Obi Bearcat Walker, and, see, Obi did most of the driving, you see. First we went on a train, and he took us in like -- see, like I say, they had these signs about white and -- and you have for blacks, then you see.

Well, Mr. Robey, he took us on this where it would say whites. He took us on the train where it would say whites, you know, and told us, well, sit down. Have a seat, you know. So we sit down. Then when the conductor come in for the tickets, conductor said to us, said, 'What are you doing sitting in here? You're not supposed to be in here.' And Mr. Robey says, 'Oh, they're with me.' So the conductor says, 'That makes no difference. They're not allowed to ride in these cars.'

So Mr. Robey got kind of angry, and he says, 'Well, look, he'd say, well, 'I'm going to return my tickets and get the money back, you know. So he went and -- they were going to New York. He tried to talk -- and the conductor wasn't having it. So he told us just, 'Come on, get off the train. So we'd get off
the train, and Mr. Robey bought this car. And --
